reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Gastric outlet obstruction caused by a large gallstone impacting in the duodenum or pyloric channel after passing through a biliary-enteric fistula
A rare proximal variant of gallstone ileus, typically affecting older patients, often women, with previous gallstone disease
Presents with vomiting, epigastric pain, early satiety, and features of gastric outlet obstruction rather than distal small bowel obstruction
Imaging may show the classic Rigler triad of pneumobilia, a bowel obstruction, and an ectopic gallstone, here in the proximal duodenum
CT is the most useful investigation to locate the stone, demonstrate the fistula, and assess the gallbladder
Endoscopy can confirm the diagnosis and, for suitable stones, allow attempts at retrieval or fragmentation
Definitive treatment is relief of the obstruction by stone extraction, with individualised decisions about whether to address the fistula and gallbladder
reference.pathophysiology: Recurrent gallbladder inflammation causes the gallbladder to adhere to and then erode into the adjacent duodenum or stomach, creating a cholecystoduodenal or cholecystogastric fistula. A large gallstone passes through this fistula directly into the proximal gastrointestinal tract and becomes impacted at the pylorus or duodenum, where the lumen is relatively narrow, producing gastric outlet obstruction. Because the stone lodges proximally rather than at the ileocaecal valve, the clinical picture is one of upper rather than lower gastrointestinal obstruction. The fistula also allows air to reflux into the biliary tree, giving the pneumobilia seen on imaging.
additionalDifferentials: Gallstone ileus with distal small bowel impaction
Malignant gastric outlet obstruction from gastric or pancreatic carcinoma
Peptic ulcer disease with pyloric stenosis
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to localise the stone, fistula, and pneumobilia
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for diagnosis and possible stone retrieval
Abdominal radiograph, which may show the Rigler triad
Blood tests including electrolytes to assess dehydration from vomiting
Ultrasound to evaluate the gallbladder and biliary tree
redFlags: Persistent vomiting with dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
Signs of duodenal perforation or peritonitis
Gastrointestinal bleeding from mucosal pressure necrosis at the impaction site
Aspiration due to a high obstruction
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is reasonable once the obstruction is relieved, but mortality is not negligible given the typically elderly, comorbid population, so a minimally invasive, staged approach that prioritises relieving the obstruction is often favoured.
pitfalls: Failing to consider a gallstone cause of gastric outlet obstruction in an older patient
Overlooking pneumobilia or an ectopic stone on imaging
Undertaking extensive combined stone and fistula surgery in a frail patient when simple stone extraction would suffice
Attributing the presentation to malignancy or peptic disease and delaying appropriate treatment
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Blumgart's Surgery of the Liver, Biliary Tract and Pancreas
management: Initial resuscitation with intravenous fluids and correction of the electrolyte disturbance caused by vomiting
Nasogastric decompression of the obstructed, distended stomach
Endoscopic stone retrieval or fragmentation by mechanical or laser lithotripsy as first-line, minimally invasive relief for accessible stones
Surgical enterolithotomy to extract the impacted gallstone when endoscopic clearance fails
A staged strategy that prioritises relieving the obstruction, with delayed or omitted cholecystectomy and fistula repair given the typically elderly, comorbid population
Perioperative optimisation of comorbidities with combined surgical and gastroenterology input
Monitoring for recurrent stone impaction and biliary complications after treatment
